paragraphs: Designing a useful optimization heuristic involves deciding how an entire algorithm should work, as well as improving its individual components. Many approaches using language models restrict generation to a fixed template so that the resulting code can run. A2DEPT addresses the resulting restriction on what kinds of algorithms the search can discover.

The method uses language models to design complete algorithms and explores candidates through an evolutionary search organized as a tree. Hybrid selection and hierarchical operators support repeated refinement at different levels of the algorithm. A lightweight maintenance loop uses execution feedback to repair generated programs, making broader exploration practical without relying on a rigid algorithmic template.

Across standard and highly constrained benchmarks, the authors report consistently better results than state-of-the-art baselines, with an average 9.8% reduction in the optimality gap. This measures improvement in how close the solutions come to the optimum. The findings support system-level algorithm generation as a viable, scalable direction for automated optimization, with executability maintained through repair during the search.
icml-2026-a-2-dept-large-language-modeld.tldr: A2DEPT evolves complete algorithms with language models and repairs execution errors, reducing the average optimality gap by 9.8% in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Intermediate representations in language and speech models can predict brain responses to language better than their output layers. This paper investigates which properties of those representations explain that correspondence. Its evidence points toward rich representations of meaning as a driver of brain alignment, rather than the models’ next-word prediction properties themselves.

The authors examine intrinsic dimension, a measure of feature complexity, across model layers. They find that it peaks in middle layers where higher-order linguistic features develop, and that it strongly predicts how well a layer explains fMRI and ECoG measurements. The relationship between intrinsic dimension and brain predictivity emerges during pretraining, connecting this correspondence to how representations develop.

The study also fine-tunes models to predict brain responses more accurately. This intervention causally increases both intrinsic dimension and semantic content in the representations. Together, the findings suggest that semantic richness, representational complexity, and brain predictivity track one another. Language modeling appears sufficiently demanding to induce this abstraction, but the authors leave open whether other tasks could induce it too.
icml-2026-abstraction-induces-the-brain-.tldr: The study links models’ ability to predict brain responses to rich meaning representations and high intrinsic dimension in intermediate layers.

paragraphs: Gromov-Wasserstein distance compares structures across different spaces by considering their internal relationships. Its global coupling also makes it sensitive to corrupted structure. The paper distinguishes noise caused by outlier nodes from noise caused by false connections between otherwise valid nodes, arguing that methods focused on adjusting node mass do not adequately handle the latter.

The proposed Structurally Robust Gromov-Wasserstein formulation introduces an adaptive dual-mask mechanism that filters geometric distortions during optimization. It preserves the strict marginal constraints of balanced transport while isolating problematic structure. The accompanying Mask-Guided GW algorithm jointly updates the transport plan, which specifies the alignment, and the filters that determine which structural information should influence it.

The authors prove convergence to a critical point using the Kurdyka-Łojasiewicz framework; this is a convergence result rather than a guarantee of a globally best alignment. Experiments on synthetic geometric matching and real-world subgraph alignment show improved alignment quality, especially with severe structural noise. The contribution is a way to address corrupted relationships without treating all affected nodes as outliers.
icml-2026-achieving-structurally-robust-.tldr: Adaptive structural masks make Gromov-Wasserstein alignment more robust to false connections while preserving balanced transport constraints.

paragraphs: When an agent learns from complete attempts at a task, its final outcome can obscure the value of individual actions. A failed attempt may contain useful progress, yet assigning credit mainly from overall success or failure makes that progress difficult to recognize. This paper develops a more detailed training signal for language-model agents.

GraphGPO combines rollout trajectories into one graph of states and transitions. It uses information across that graph to estimate how far each state is from the task goal. Each transition then receives a graph-based advantage according to how much it reduces the estimated distance. This makes the training signal depend on a step’s contribution to progress, informed by the other collected trajectories.

The authors report substantially improved training efficiency and state-of-the-art performance across challenging benchmarks. The approach matters because it reuses relationships among collected attempts to extract information that final outcomes alone do not provide. In particular, a useful transition can receive credit even when the trajectory containing it ultimately fails, addressing the specific attribution problem that motivates the method.
icml-2026-beyond-trajectory-level-attrib.tldr: GraphGPO combines agent trajectories into a graph and rewards individual transitions for reducing their estimated distance to the goal.

paragraphs: Time series forecasting requires interpreting contextual information and modeling uncertain changes in continuous values. CoGenCast combines these capabilities in a generative framework. The paper motivates the combination by arguing that autoregressive language models and diffusion-like generators, when used alone, do not adequately address both contextual understanding and continuous probabilistic dynamics.

The method changes the attention topology of a pretrained decoder-only language model to create a forecasting encoder-decoder backbone. This allows bidirectional encoding of context alongside causal generation of representations. A flow-matching component then models continuous temporal evolution, conditioned on the representations generated autoregressively. The two components therefore take complementary roles within the same forecasting process.

CoGenCast also supports multimodal forecasting and unified training across domains. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show performance competitive with previous baselines, supporting the usefulness of combining contextual representations with a continuous generative mechanism. The stated result is competitive forecasting performance rather than universal superiority, and the framework’s broader contribution is a common architecture for handling these two aspects of prediction together.
icml-2026-cogencast-a-coupled-autoregres.tldr: CoGenCast couples a reconfigured pretrained language model with flow matching to forecast continuous time series using contextual information.

paragraphs: Cross-modal retrieval uses representations that make related items from different modalities searchable together. Proxy-based hashing learns these representations with reference points called proxies. The paper identifies a weakness in methods that constrain similarity to each proxy separately: although the proxies are trained jointly, their responses do not explicitly compete or express relationships during optimization.

The proposed method organizes several proxies into a relational structure specific to each sample. Structure-guided learning then contrasts positive and negative proxy responses, instead of simply accumulating their effects. This interaction is intended to define clearer decision regions in the Hamming space where the learned binary representations are compared, giving retrieval a more discriminative organization.

Experiments on standard cross-modal benchmarks show consistent improvements in retrieval accuracy and separation between embeddings. These findings support the paper’s central claim that the relationships among proxies are useful training information. The contribution concerns how reference points interact around a sample: explicitly contrasting their responses improves the structure of the representation used to distinguish relevant from irrelevant retrieval results.
icml-2026-deep-discriminative-structure-.tldr: Making hashing proxies interact and compete for each sample produces clearer representation boundaries and improves cross-modal retrieval.

paragraphs: Choosing a face recognition dataset usually requires judging whether it can support a strong model before committing substantial training resources. This paper proposes Intrinsic Quality, or IQ, as a validation-free estimate of that potential. Its aim is to make dataset diagnosis and curation possible without first carrying out full-scale model training.

IQ combines two views of the data. A Neighbor-Consistency Score checks whether nearby examples in the representation space agree on identity labels. Effective rank summarizes the complexity of the global representation subspace, capturing aspects of geometry and diversity. Combining these components gives the metric information about both local label agreement and the broader structure of the dataset.

The proposed evaluation can use lightweight proxy models or subsets of the data, making it suitable for an early screening stage. The authors describe a protocol covering clean, noisy, and mixed-quality datasets and outline ways to test whether IQ predicts downstream performance. The abstract presents a metric and validation methodology, rather than reporting demonstrated predictive accuracy, so its contribution is a concrete approach to cheaper dataset assessment.
icml-2026-efficient-validation-free-intr.tldr: IQ proposes combining local identity-label consistency and global representation diversity to assess face recognition datasets before full-scale training.

paragraphs: This paper treats documentation for coding agents as executable guidance whose quality is measured by the correctness of the code it helps produce. Its central difficulty is dependency coupling: improving guidance for one program entity can invalidate guidance for entities that call it. Repeated local refinements can consequently keep creating problems elsewhere.

DocSearch addresses this with two levels of search. The outer level follows the program’s dependency graph, refining callees before their callers to avoid downstream interference. The inner level uses beam search to explore candidate documentation refinements. It draws varied error messages from self-generated unit tests, using that diagnostic feedback to guide exploration and move beyond locally attractive refinements.

On DevEval+, DocSearch reaches a 90.7% solve rate with GPT-4o and reports outperforming the strongest baseline by 32.6%. Cross-language experiments also show that the optimized documentation transfers effectively to other target programming languages. The findings support optimizing documentation through code outcomes and dependency structure, making it a practical control mechanism for coding agents rather than evaluating it solely for readability.
icml-2026-escaping-whack-a-mole-optimizi.tldr: DocSearch optimizes agent-facing documentation using dependency order and test feedback, reaching a reported 90.7% solve rate on DevEval+.

paragraphs: Image-to-point cloud registration matches an image with a three-dimensional point cloud. Viewpoint changes, differences between the two data types, and repeated textures can create ambiguity about scale and produce incorrect matches. The paper targets remaining weaknesses in detection-free approaches that already use features at multiple scales and transformer interactions.

FS-I2P introduces a Focus–Sweep approach through a Hierarchical Mamba Interaction Module in a state-space-model framework. This module strengthens associations between image and point-cloud features at multiple levels. The design addresses attention drifting across layers and inconsistent associations within a scale, both of which the authors identify as obstacles to precise registration.

A Dynamic Layer Allocation Strategy additionally adapts the number of processing iterations to make better use of geometric constraints and improve matching robustness. Experiments and ablations on RGB-D Scenes V2 and 7-Scenes show state-of-the-art performance. The contribution combines improved cross-modal interaction with adaptive processing depth, treating both feature association and the amount of iterative refinement as important parts of obtaining reliable correspondences.
icml-2026-fs-i2p-a-hierarchical-focusswe.tldr: FS-I2P combines hierarchical image–point cloud interactions with adaptive iteration depth to improve registration on two benchmarks.

paragraphs: Text-to-image models can produce realistic, prompt-consistent images while still reproducing societal biases. HoloFair addresses the difficulty of evaluating those biases across multiple demographic attributes and socially meaningful conditions. The paper argues that assessments focused on a single dimension can overlook deeper patterns in what a model generates.

The evaluation framework combines a large fairness-oriented dataset with SpaFreq, a classifier for attributes based on spatial and frequency information. Its Multi-attribute, Group-wise Bias Index is designed to measure both intrinsic diversity and conditional biases. This brings questions about overall representation and representation under particular conditions into the same assessment framework.

The paper also introduces Fair-GRPO, which uses reinforcement learning and a multi-objective reward to change the model’s generation distribution. Experiments on SD3.5-Medium show substantial improvements in multidimensional fairness while maintaining high image quality. The authors additionally analyze potential reward hacking and provide mitigation strategies, recognizing that optimizing a fairness reward can produce behavior that exploits the reward rather than fulfilling its intended purpose.
icml-2026-holofair-unified-t2i-fairness-.tldr: HoloFair evaluates multidimensional demographic bias, while Fair-GRPO improves measured fairness through reinforcement learning with a multi-objective reward.

paragraphs: Diffusion policies can represent several distinct modes of action, giving reinforcement learning more flexibility than a unimodal Gaussian policy. This paper investigates how to use that flexibility for safe learning in online settings. It proposes Augmented Lagrangian-Guided Diffusion, or ALGD, as an off-policy algorithm that incorporates safety into diffusion-based policy generation.

The authors interpret the Lagrangian, which combines the optimization objective with constraints, as an energy function guiding denoising. Their analysis traces instability in primal–dual methods to the non-convex shape of that energy landscape. Directly using the Lagrangian as diffusion guidance can therefore destabilize both the generation of actions and the learning process.

ALGD introduces an augmented Lagrangian that locally makes the energy landscape convex, stabilizing generation and training without changing the distribution of the optimal policy. This local modification is central to the method’s theoretical rationale. Theoretical analysis and extensive experiments support the approach, with strong and stable performance across diverse environments. The result connects the geometry of constrained optimization to the behavior of a diffusion policy.
icml-2026-how-does-the-lagrangian-guide-.tldr: ALGD stabilizes safe diffusion-policy learning by locally convexifying its guiding energy landscape while preserving the optimal policy distribution.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires a model to learn new classes while retaining useful earlier knowledge. CLIP-based approaches often freeze the pretrained backbone to limit forgetting, but this restricts adaptation to downstream tasks. HypCL introduces a parameter-efficient way to adapt CLIP continually using hyperbolic geometry, with the aim of learning more discriminative features.

The method attaches task-specific adapters and composes their updates sequentially within the Poincaré ball, a representation of hyperbolic space. Its motivation is the space’s exponentially expanding capacity, which can accommodate a growing set of classes and encourage stronger separation between them. Geometry therefore becomes part of how the method organizes accumulating task knowledge.

HypCL also maintains visual prototypes computed from the adapted features. These serve as stable reference points for calibrating predictions during inference, making use of the separation developed in hyperbolic space. Experiments on standard class-incremental benchmarks show consistent improvements over existing CLIP-based continual learning methods. The findings support combining task-specific adaptation, hyperbolic representations, and prototype-based calibration when the set of classes expands over time.
icml-2026-hypcl-adapting-clip-in-hyperbo.tldr: HypCL adapts CLIP with task-specific updates in hyperbolic space and uses visual prototypes to improve continual classification.

paragraphs: Compressing a long reasoning trace into a few latent tokens can make language-model reasoning more efficient. The paper argues that reconstructing the original text during compression also pressures those tokens to preserve wording and syntax. That emphasis on linguistic form can limit how well they abstract the overall structure of the reasoning.

ImgCoT changes the reconstruction target to an image rendered from the reasoning text. The resulting spatial bias encourages the compressed representation to capture how reasoning steps are arranged. The method is intended to retain global reasoning structure with fewer tokens, shifting what the compression process is encouraged to preserve.

The authors also acknowledge that visual latent tokens can blur important details. Their loose ImgCoT variant therefore adds a small number of textual reasoning steps selected using low token log-likelihood. This hybrid combines a compact visual representation with selected fine-grained information while still using fewer tokens than the complete reasoning trace. Experiments across multiple datasets and language models demonstrate the effectiveness of both versions, supporting the choice of reconstruction target as a useful design decision.
icml-2026-imgcot-compressing-long-chain-.tldr: ImgCoT compresses reasoning through image reconstruction, with a hybrid variant retaining selected textual steps to preserve details.

paragraphs: A fixed sampling budget for language-model reinforcement learning can be spent on more attempts per problem, more problems per batch, or more update steps. This paper studies how to allocate that budget for on-policy training. It frames these choices as a constrained optimization problem, seeking useful allocation rules rather than simply recommending more computation.

The authors find that the compute-optimal number of parallel rollouts per problem rises predictably with the available budget and eventually saturates. The pattern appears for both easy and hard problems, but with different explanations: sharpening solutions on easy problems and expanding solution coverage on hard ones. These distinctions connect the allocation rule to what additional samples accomplish.

More parallel rollouts also reduce interference across problems, while the number of problems in a batch mainly influences training stability and can vary over a broad range. Validation across base models and data distributions supports the practical usefulness of these findings. The resulting guidance treats rollout count as a budget-dependent decision and batch problem count as a comparatively flexible stability choice.
icml-2026-isocompute-playbook-optimally-.tldr: The study finds budget-dependent rules for allocating RL sampling compute, with optimal rollouts per problem increasing and then saturating.

paragraphs: A model’s current performance does not directly reveal how readily it can adapt to a new task. This capacity, called plasticity, matters for continual and transfer learning. The paper introduces local redundancy to measure it, motivated by the weak theoretical grounding and poor downstream correlations of measures such as effective rank, dead neuron fraction, and weight norm.

Local redundancy comes from universal compression theory. It considers the worst-case redundancy of a model family formed by infinitesimal parameter changes along gradient directions. Exact computation is intractable, so the authors derive a practical lower bound: the expected squared gradient norm on a synthetic memorization task. This gives an efficiently measurable quantity with a formal connection to the proposed plasticity measure.

Experiments in continual image classification and time series transfer learning show better prediction of downstream performance than existing measures. The approach also supports choosing pretraining checkpoints when validation loss has plateaued. That finding matters because checkpoints with similar validation loss can still differ in their usefulness for later adaptation, and the proposed measure provides additional information for selecting among them.
icml-2026-local-redundancy-an-informatio.tldr: Local redundancy gives a theoretically motivated measure of adaptability, with a computable lower bound derived from synthetic memorization gradients.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can attend to an image and still generate claims unsupported by it. This paper identifies route competition as a key failure mode: the textual pathway can dominate the final token decision even when visual tokens receive attention. Consequently, observing visual attention alone does not establish that the image determined the answer.

The proposed intervention separates each attention head into visual and text routes. An efficient approximation using one forward pass and one gradient estimates their effects on individual token decisions. Those estimates expose conflicts between routes and identify heads dominated by linguistic priors. The method then selectively suppresses the text route in those heads while leaving the visual route intact.

This intervention requires no training and acts during inference. Across five benchmarks covering discriminative and generative tasks, it consistently reduces hallucination-related errors across models, with limited effects on overall multimodal performance and modest inference overhead. The findings support targeting how text and visual evidence influence the actual decision, making the intervention more selective than suppressing an entire attention head.
icml-2026-mitigating-hallucinations-in-l.tldr: A training-free intervention reduces visual hallucinations by selectively suppressing text pathways that overpower image evidence during token decisions.

paragraphs: A diffusion model serving several tasks must balance multiple target distributions. Achieving good trade-offs can require a generalist model much larger than a model sufficient for any single task, potentially increasing data requirements. This paper studies that problem when paired training examples are scarce but unlabeled conditioning data are abundant.

The proposed procedure first trains lightweight specialist models using the limited paired data. It then generates pseudo-samples to distill those specialists into a generalist. The authors establish generalization bounds in which the required number of paired samples depends only on the complexity of the specialist model classes. This separates that labeled-data requirement from the larger capacity needed for the generalist.

The theory also covers diffusion policies for sequential decisions, accounting for distribution shifts during on-policy rollouts. Experiments on robotic control and image restoration are used to verify the theoretical results. The contribution is therefore both a training strategy and a statistical explanation of how abundant conditioning data and specialist-generated samples can support multi-objective diffusion learning under the stated semi-supervised setting.
icml-2026-multi-objective-learning-for-d.tldr: Training specialists before distilling a generalist yields diffusion-learning bounds whose paired-data requirements depend on specialist complexity.

paragraphs: Electron density provides a physically grounded input for predicting material properties, but large datasets and efficient representations have been difficult to obtain. VisionED addresses both barriers for organic materials. The authors curate two million molecules and encode electron density as multi-shot images that capture geometric and electronic structure.

The model is pretrained on 12 million such images using physics-informed tasks across scales. Evaluations on photovoltaic and organic chromophore datasets show improvements of up to 27.0% over state-of-the-art baselines, alongside stronger robustness to distribution shifts and limited data. These results support using electron-density images as an effective input modality for the evaluated property-prediction tasks.

The authors also report generalization to unseen device-scale applications, recovering experimental trends and mixing-ratio effects in ternary blends with 92.77% average accuracy. Compared with the previous electron-density point-cloud representation, the image representation improves performance by 26.2%, with memory and time reductions reported as factors of 2.6 and 4.6. The contribution connects physical information with an image representation that is both predictive and computationally more efficient in the reported comparisons.
icml-2026-physics-informed-pre-training-.tldr: VisionED pretrains on electron-density images to improve organic-material property prediction while reducing representation costs.

paragraphs: Personalized agents handle sensitive information whose appropriate use depends on context. Privacy failures can therefore arise through an agent’s actions even when the relevant privacy expectations are implicit. PrivAct addresses this problem through learning, motivated by the brittleness, scenario dependence, and potentially expanded attack surface of external interventions applied during inference.

The framework uses preference training to embed contextual privacy preferences into each agent’s generation behavior. Its aim is to improve contextual integrity across a multi-agent system while retaining helpfulness. Training each participant makes privacy-aware behavior part of how the system produces actions, addressing the distributed nature of information handling across interacting agents.

Experiments across several language-model backbones and benchmarks show consistent improvements in contextual privacy preservation. Reported leakage reductions reach up to 12.32%, while helpfulness remains comparable. The evaluations also show zero-shot generalization and robustness across different multi-agent topologies. These findings support preference training as a way to improve the privacy-helpfulness trade-off, with the reported gains extending across several tested models and interaction structures.
icml-2026-privact-internalizing-contextu.tldr: PrivAct trains contextual privacy preferences into interacting agents, reducing reported leakage while maintaining comparable helpfulness.

paragraphs: Safety interventions during text generation often react to a local warning sign after an unsafe response has begun. Under adversarial prompting, repairing the latest problem can still leave generation prone to repeating the violation. RBCBF addresses both where to rewind a response and how to change generation after that rewind.

The framework treats a terminal violation as the result of risk accumulated across the generated prefix. It uses this aggregated view to identify decisive prefixes and select rollback points, making the choice depend on the trajectory rather than isolated heuristic cues. After rollback, it directly corrects the next-token distribution under multiple rule constraints.

The combination matters because returning to an earlier point and changing subsequent generation are complementary parts of repair. Across jailbreak-style evaluations, RBCBF outperforms previous rollback methods and decoding-time baselines, reducing harmful responses and substantially lowering recurring violations. These results support using trajectory-level risk to target an intervention and distribution-level control to make the repaired continuation less likely to repeat the same safety failure.
icml-2026-rbcbf-decoding-time-safety-ali.tldr: RBCBF uses accumulated generation risk to choose rollback points and correct token distributions, reducing harmful responses and repeated violations.

paragraphs: Gradual domain adaptation moves a model from a source distribution toward a target through intermediate domains. When useful real intermediates are unavailable, they must be synthesized. The paper argues that training flow-based generators through sample-based likelihood estimation can discard information useful for adaptation, motivating an approach that constructs intermediates directly from samples.

E-SUOT reformulates flow-based gradual adaptation as a Lagrangian dual problem and derives an equivalent semi-dual objective that avoids likelihood estimation. This formulation creates a new difficulty: unstable min–max optimization. The authors add entropy regularization to turn the training process into a more stable sequence of optimization steps.

The resulting framework uses entropy-regularized semi-dual unbalanced optimal transport to construct intermediate domains and support adaptation. The paper provides theoretical analyses of stability and generalization, together with extensive experiments demonstrating efficacy. Its contribution links the construction of synthetic intermediate data to the optimization procedure used to obtain them, addressing information loss and training instability within the same framework rather than treating them as unrelated issues.
icml-2026-rethinking-the-flow-based-grad.tldr: E-SUOT constructs intermediate adaptation domains without likelihood estimation and uses entropy regularization to stabilize optimization.

paragraphs: Explaining a prediction on a temporal graph requires identifying which interactions matter over time. This paper separates recurring interactions, called stability patterns, from newly appearing interactions, called transition patterns. It argues that existing explanations concentrate on the former and overlook the latter, even though both are needed for faithful temporal explanations.

ST-TGExplainer builds explanation into a temporal graph neural network. It learns a compact explanatory subgraph using a disentangled information bottleneck objective. The objective keeps information useful for predicting the event label while explicitly reducing redundancy between stability and transition patterns, conditioned on that label. This encourages the two kinds of evidence to make distinct contributions to the explanation.

Extensive experiments show strong predictive performance and more faithful explanations. The findings support distinguishing persistent relationships from emerging ones when explaining temporal predictions. The compact subgraph is intended to preserve the evidence relevant to the event, while the redundancy constraint prevents the two pattern categories from simply duplicating each other’s explanatory information. Prediction and explanation are thus learned together within the model.
icml-2026-st-tgexplainer-disentangling-s.tldr: ST-TGExplainer learns compact temporal-graph explanations that separate recurring interactions from newly emerging ones.

paragraphs: Self-play preference optimization trains a language model on win–lose comparisons between its own responses. This paper identifies a failure mode when the preference oracle confidently favors one response over another with essentially the same meaning. Those overconfident distinctions can destabilize optimization and cause the policy’s performance to deteriorate.

S-SPPO calibrates both supervision and internal representations. Semantic gating moves win-rate targets toward the maximum-entropy baseline as response meanings overlap, weakening unjustified preference certainty. A latent repulsion mechanism maintains geometric diversity between chosen and rejected samples, addressing collapse in the representation space. Together, the components adjust both the learning signal and the representations affected by it.

The theoretical analysis shows that calibration preserves the constant-sum game structure, facilitating convergence to a Nash equilibrium. Empirically, S-SPPO avoids the degradation observed in prior methods. With Llama-3-8B, it reaches a 52.19% win rate and 47.46% length-controlled win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 without additional human-annotated training preferences. The findings support accounting for semantic equivalence when generating preference supervision through self-play.
icml-2026-textits-sppo-semantic-calibrat.tldr: S-SPPO stabilizes self-play preference learning by reducing overconfident judgments between similar responses and preserving representation diversity.

paragraphs: Learning to select branching variables and cutting planes often means imitating local expert scores. This paper shows why accurate imitation alone does not guarantee a small branch-and-cut search tree. Its theoretical results identify two problems: the expert signal can be misaligned with tree size, and recursive search can amplify tiny decision differences.

For cut selection, optimizing improvement in the linear-programming bound can produce an exponentially larger strong-branching tree than a simple proxy score. The paper also notes that strong branching itself can be exponentially suboptimal. Separately, arbitrarily small changes to a root cut set’s right-hand sides can change the minimum tree size from one node to exponentially many.

Branching decisions exhibit similar sensitivity: tiny score discrepancies, different tie-breaking, or even a small number of differing decisions along a trajectory can yield exponentially different tree sizes. These are possibility results, not a claim that every learned policy suffers such growth. They establish that local score accuracy is insufficient as a guarantee and motivate learning objectives more directly aligned with the overall search tree.
icml-2026-theoretical-challenges-in-lear.tldr: Theoretical examples show that accurate local branch-and-cut scores can still lead to exponentially larger search trees.

paragraphs: Relational deep learning converts database tables and their relationships into graphs for graph neural networks. This paper asks whether the graph implied by a database schema is also suitable for a particular prediction task. It identifies two systematic problems with direct conversion: too much irrelevant information and fragmented semantic relationships.

An empirical study of real-world databases finds that effective graphs require a task-dependent balance between removing irrelevant structure and adding useful relational connections. More filtering does not consistently mean better performance. Likewise, adding connections helps only when they reflect the downstream task’s logic. The graph should therefore be adapted according to what the model needs to predict.

The authors build an end-to-end structural optimizer that performs both filtering and structural injection automatically. Across 23 classification, regression, and recommendation tasks, the resulting graphs consistently improve accuracy and often lower inference cost. These findings make graph construction part of the learning problem: selecting and connecting relevant relational information can improve both predictive quality and, in many tested cases, the cost of using the model.
icml-2026-what-makes-a-desired-graph-for.tldr: Task-aware removal and addition of graph structure improves relational prediction, with optimized graphs often reducing inference cost.
